analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates on public companies with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps and favors low-gap firms in federal contracting.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would raise corporate tax rates for firms with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps and favor low-gap firms for federal contracts, was introduced in May 2021 and referred to two House committees but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the corporate income tax rate on publicly traded companies whose CEO or highest-paid employee earns more than 100 times what their typical US employee makes, with the surcharge growing as the pay gap widens. It would also add a 50% tax-rate increase for companies that cut their US workforce by more than 10% while increasing contracted or foreign workers. Finally, it would require federal agencies to prefer contractors whose pay ratio is below 50-to-1 when evaluating bids.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large public companies, who would benefit from pressure on their employers to narrow executive-to-worker pay gaps or to keep jobs in the United States rather than outsource them. Taxpayers would benefit from modestly higher corporate tax revenue from the widest-gap firms, and taxpayers generally would gain from federal contracting dollars flowing preferentially to companies that pay their rank-and-file workers proportionately better.

how_it_helps.text: Publicly traded companies whose CEO or highest-paid employee earns more than 100 times their median US employee's pay would pay a higher corporate income tax rate, with the surcharge rising from 0.5 points (over 100-to-1) to 3 points (over 400-to-1).
If a company cuts its US full-time workforce by more than 10% while adding contracted or foreign workers, the tax surcharge would be increased by 50%.

Federal agencies would give preference in contract bids to companies whose pay ratio was below 50-to-1 the previous year, steering taxpayer money toward firms that pay their workers closer to what they pay executives.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations with extreme pay gaps, whose tax bills would rise, and large firms that shrink their US workforce while outsourcing or offshoring, which would face a steeper tax increase. Companies competing for federal contracts with pay ratios above 50-to-1 would face a disadvantage in bidding.

drawbacks.text: The tax surcharge tops out at 3 additional percentage points, which is small relative to the tens or hundreds of millions some CEOs are paid, so it may change little at the companies with the widest gaps.

The penalty for shifting work abroad or to contractors adds 50% to the pay-ratio surcharge, and the detailed employee-counting definitions could be complicated to administer and might penalize legitimate restructurings.

Because it applies only to publicly traded corporations, the highest ratio could be dodged by going private, shifting compensation into equity structures, or moving work to subsidiaries outside the controlled group's reporting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefits—slightly higher corporate tax for extreme pay-gap companies and a contracting preference for fair-pay firms—are real but modest in size: a few percentage points of tax and a tie-breaking edge in procurement. The mechanism is well designed in that it uses companies' own SEC-reported pay data and targets only very large pay gaps, not ordinary pay differences. The strongest objection is complexity and possible gaming: firms could shift pay through contractors or relocate work to avoid the threshold, and the 50% rate add-on for replacing US workers is a blunt tool that could be hard to administer. The bill's bigger shortcoming is that it never received any committee action or vote, so no refinement or public airing of these tradeoffs ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Oversight committees in May 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2021, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Oversight and Reform Committee the same day.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it never moved in the Senate because no Senate version advanced.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, at which point the bill died without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies with very high executive pay and their shareholders are better off, since the tax surcharge and contracting preference were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-ratio public companies and their shareholders

for.name: 9 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over corporate tax rates
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it—no hearing, markup, or vote—during the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee
against.role: Second committee of jurisdiction over the contracting provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats and the sole sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced past referral in a Democratic-controlled House.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations with wide pay gaps
industries.note: Firms with CEO-to-median-worker pay ratios above 100-to-1 would pay a higher corporate tax rate, and those shrinking US staff while adding outsourced or foreign workers would pay an even higher surcharge [S3].
Contractors would face a new evaluation factor: those with pay ratios under 50-to-1 would gain an edge in winning federal contracts, while wide-gap firms would be disadvantaged [S2].

Executives at high-ratio firms would face shareholder pressure to narrow pay gaps to avoid the tax surcharge; compensation advisory firms would gain work helping companies measure and report ratios under the new definitions [S3].
